BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.


Boston, Sept. 6.—The expected withdrawal of the
Hon. Thomas Talbot was made public to-day in
letter from Mr. Talbot to Major George S. Merrill
Secretary of the Republican State Committee. Mr.
Talbot says that it is the duty of the party to make
such an administration as shall best conduce to en-
tire harmony. As contribution to that result he
will not allow his name to be presented to the Con-
vention. The letter is as follows:


Boston, Sept. 6, 1875.
Maj. GEORGE S. MERRILL, Secretary of the Republican
STATE: As my name has been freely used in connec-
tion with the nomination of the Republican PARTY, I
must make frank statement through you as the Secretary OF
the party organization. The importance of the approach-
ing convention cannot be overstated. Should I occupy
an equivocal position regarding the restoration of our
currency to a sound basis as the only means of reviving
trade and insuring the continued prosperity of the
country, and to the advancement of the standard of
public virtue, by furthering all the moral and religious
principles, I must make such a governmental nomination as shall best con-
duce to the entire harmony of the party. In the statement of the only question up on which
views upon the subject, my own judgment leads
me to concur with those who believe that
the best interests of temperance demand that
the present law for the regulation of the
liquor traffic should receive fair, thorough, and impartial trials; and though whole influence and honest
efforts be applied to this end, I can but recognize
the fact that my pronounced views upon this question
might, in the nomination, create doubts as to
the integrity of purposes and give rise to suspicion that
the experiment would not receive a fair trial at my
hands. Should widespread distrust, born of such
doubts and suspicions, manifest itself at the election, the
party might not only receive a severe
check, but breach its influence in the state, the consequences of
which would be disastrous both at home and abroad.
To avoid this, far as may lie my power, I prefer to
sacrifice my personal aspirations for a triumph dearer to me than my own indi-
vidual success.


While I therefore appreciate sincerely the kind sup-
port of friends, who would earnestly press me, I must
inform the party I will not allow its use in the approaching convention
as a candidate for the nomination for the office of Governor.
Very truly yours, THOMAS TALBOT.

The letter excites nothing but favorable comment;
it simplifies the situation without helping the
chances either of Mr. Rice or Mr. Loving.

for you, Sire, chastising their bodies instead

beloved Fatherland, where again is the
danger to the State?

name to them? It was not the fear of dan-
ger to the State that led your counsellors to

revenge, still less that of the poor exiles.

life; and if, when weighed in the
balance you are found wanting, you will

avenger. His Eye will seek and His Hand
will strike the prosecutors of those who
have consecrated themselves to His ser-
vice.

time of which Felix the Governor spoke,

be entreated, implored to return, but who
knows whether the convenient time for
the Governor will also be the convenient
time for his Lord and Master—for God may
then turn a deaf ear and not allow these
angels in the flesh to return to the land where

land which exiles beings such as these?"

A charge was made against her of having poisoned the cook, whose body was disinterred for examination; but decomposition had gone too far for analysis to produce any results. Some evidence was offered to the Judge of instruction that the prisoner had been heard to say Hemlock was very safe poison to use, but he did not see grounds to sustain the capital charge, which was accordingly abandoned.

The Court sentenced the false countess to ten years of that intermediate imprisonment between simple confinement and hard labor called "reclusion," which will not admit her being treated as first-class misdemeanant.

ANOTHER MURDER DEVELOPED—A PROBABLE PARALLEL TO THE UNDERTOOK CASE.

Peaceful Chester county, so free from common rowdyism or lawlessness, and yet so prolific in bloody murders, is now agitated with the finding of a man's body in the Brandywine at Mortonville, bearing many evidences of foul play. The supposed murder, which possesses many of the mysterious phases of the Liddersook-Goss tragedy, is thus given by the West Chester Local News, of yesterday:

We learn that the body of a middle aged man was found in the dam at Mortonville, last evening, and owing to its decomposed state it had not been identified when our informant left that village. It was found lying in shallow water, partly surrounded and covered with "splatter docks" and from another source we are informed a bullet hole was found in the skull, which would strongly argue that foul play was the cause of death. The features were terribly disfigured, and it is said the body must have been in the water at least two weeks. The body was noticed by several persons at different times, but they supposed it was a log of wood, and consequently gave the matter no further consideration.

The body was first discovered by the son of Mr. Eber Smith, miller at Mortonville who was going up the dam for the purpose of looking after some traps he had set on its upper banks. The corpse was brought to his view by the action of the waves caused by the motion of the boat, and upon the boy seeing it he was very much frightened and at once turned back and hurriedly communicated the intelligence to his father.

Mr. Smith at once sent an employee in company with young man named Chas. Etter to the scene, where by the aid of a hook they soon succeeded in pulling the body into the boat, and from thence they conveyed it to the Railroad Station House, where it yet remains. Deputy Coroner Lewis of Coatesville was at once notified, and upon appearing at the scene empannelled a jury of inquest, and in the meantime the professional services of Dr. Palmer of Doe Run, and Dr. Harry of Coatesville were enlisted in the investigation. Upon making an examination of the body a pistol-ball hole was found in the centre of the forehead which upon being probed, was found to characterize beyond all doubt. Another wound was found upon his left arm, but not of serious nature.

Some ten days ago a good and nearly new silk hat was picked up near the water tank, about six hundred yards above the place where the body was found, and the only conclusion to be arrived at is that the stranger has been murdered and afterwards thrown into the Brandywine near the water tank from which point the body drifted down to the place where it was discovered by the boy Smith on Tuesday morning.

His clothing is new in part, the boots having the appearance of only having been worn few days, and the same may be said of his shirt, the band of which was fastened by a gold button. He had on two coats, both of which were buttoned tight up to his chin. In one of the pockets of the undercoat a stone was found, weighing five or 8 pounds. No clue was found in his pockets, and nothing has as yet been discovered to lead to the identification of the body.

The jury remained in session until yesterday afternoon, at 4 o'clock, when it adjourned to meet again this morning at 8.30 o'clock. The deceased when living must have measured five feet eleven inches, and weighed about one hundred and eighty pounds. He wore full dark whiskers, had broad high forehead, and evidence yet remains that his appearance was of highly genteel order.

CHINESE PRIVATE LIFE.—Here are some
hints which may be useful to some of our
cooks: They have a large screen before the
doorway, which gives privacy sufficient for
their need. The window sashes are closed
either by sort of jalousie or thin matting.
They do not surround their domesticities with
the same mystery and secret precautions with
which we envelop these proceedings in Europe.
Human nature, they argue, has to sleep, and
here is the mat upon which it stretches itself.
Why conceal it? It also wants to eat, and it
satisfies its appetite no matter how many eyes
are gazing. Tell Chinese cook you are hungry,
and he will immediately fetch his fire, his
cooking utensils, his provisions, and cook under
your very nose. He has no idea of concealing
his operations in some far away back region,
yclept kitchen. He squats down anywhere,
makes fire on or in anything, basin, dish,
pan or pot—there is no limit to his invention.
He will cook in the middle of the street, or in
the centre of his guests in a restaurant. Upon
one occasion, when on board junk, observed
a man cooking his own and his neighbour's food
together in tub, and an earthenware saucer
containing the charcoal. Wonderful creatures
they are, these despised Chinese, with a deft
ness of finger and ingenuity of patience unsurpassed by any nation under the sun.—TempL

A young Swede walked into the police
headquarters at st. Paul few days ago,
and inquired for the Chief That gentle
man responded in person and be then re-
quested secret interview. The parties
retired to the private sanctunl, where
they we're closeted for a considerable
time, keeping the reporters and other out
sidcrs on the dragged edge After some
time the door was opened, and the Chief
made his appearance, but declined for
some time to render any information
relative to the private caucus, After
some time, however, he thawed out, and
furnished the following particulars to a
reporter of the DIsPATCB.


lie said that when he went into his
private room he was knocked into a
cooked hat metaphorically by the open
ing sentences Of his visitor, who said
"Chief, am come to surrender myself to
you. committed murder in New York
some years ago and cannot rest" The
Chiefs eyes sparkled. He thought he
was on the track OF the athan murderer
sure, and visions Of those twenty-five
thousand dollars which are awaiting the
discovery Of the perpetrator Of that crime
doomed up before him; but these visions
were ruthlessly dispelled by the next few
words which fell from the self.accused
murderer's lips.


The Chief asked him to give the par
ticulars of the murder and he made the
following statement:


81 came to this country in the year
1857, and got work in the book bindery
of Smith x Miller, l8 North William
Street, New York, and boarded in Vande-
water street; my name is George John
son, native of Sweden. Sometime in
October or November of that year, after
had been about three months in the
country, | went down one evening to the
battery for a walk. Returning thought
| would pay a visit to friend Of mine re-
siding on Rector street and went up West
street on the North River for that pur-
pore; had money about me, and walked
along the river bank. | had proceeded
but short distance when | met q man
who attacked me without any provoca-
ton, suppose to rob me. We had a
fight and cenched, when | got
him down. lie had hold Of
my ClOLDes Out Il managed
to shake him loose and then rolled him
into the river. After throwing him into

Among other curiosities in naval architecture which Messrs. Yarrow & Co., of London, have turned out from their establishment is a new torpedo vessel, which has attracted some attention in London. She is a small craft, long and slim, with raking funnels amidships and a top-heavy bowsprit, along which run mysterious wires, protruding from her bows. The torpedo carried at the end of a pole projecting from the bow is intended for sudden attack or for chasing the enemy. The torpedo pole, with the torpedo secured at the end, is lowered at will under the surface of the water when the boat is going into action, and the moment it comes into contact with the sides of the enemy's ship the explosion takes place.

Of course, the results of the explosion depend upon the composition of the torpedo and its size; but one important fact connected with it is that as the explosion occurs at the instant of actual contact with the "skin" of the ship, the effect is far greater than if any intervening space of water existed. It is said to have been found that for usual charges, if the explosion takes place ten feet below the surface of the water whilst the pole projects some twenty-five feet from the bows, no danger need be apprehended to the launch if well-built and skillfully handled. In the present case the torpedo is exploded not by percussion but by electricity, and as the electric circuit is completed by contact with the enemy, the advantage of the percussion system in causing explosion at the exact moment is aimed, whilst at the same time the galvanic battery placed in the launch can be connected or disconnected at pleasure.

In going into action the crew are protected from rifle shots by suitable sliding shields of steel. The present launch is 55 in length, by seven feet beam, and built throughout of mild steel iron and steel. She is partially decked, and propelled by a pair of high-pressure engines, indicating 60 horse power, and can attain such speed as to accomplish a continuous run of 20 miles in five hours. Her builders state, that they are prepared to construct launches for torpedo service of 100 feet long with the extraordinary speed of 15 miles an hour. The torpedo itself is made of stout copper capable of containing 66 pounds of dynamite (gun-cotton equal to 300 pounds of gunpowder) or other explosive. It is arranged to fire electrically, both by contact and at will.

The front part of the torpedo is fitted with a contact circuit closer, two insulated wires, which pass through the charge in the torpedo, a connection with the battery in the boat. The electric platinum fuse is attached to the return wire in the center of the torpedo charge, and an extra wire is attached to the return wire a little forward of the fuse. This wire is also connected with the battery, and has attached to it a hand circuit closer for firing at will, both the contact and hand circuit closers acting on the same fuse. The hand circuit closer consists of a small ebonite cylinder, with spring, which only needs to be pressed down in order to effect an explosion, the result of which would be to blow a hole five feet square in a ship sheathed with one-inch iron. Mr.. j. GREGORY, few years ago,
moved from Tennessee and bought
a plantation in Murray County, Ga.
The land at he time he purchased it
with good season, would produce ten
bushels of wheat to the acre. In Octo-
Der Mr.. Gregory sowed broadcast fifteen
acres of white Boughton wheat, one
bushel to the acre, and in February fol
lowing he sowed the same ground in red
clover, sowing broadcast in two ways,
one bushel to eight acres. He harvested
ten bushels of wheat per acre and cut a
fine crop of hay the same season. The
next year he moved two crops of good
clover hay, averaging two tons per acre.
The third crop grew up from four to
eight inches high, and in October he
plowed the clover under, blowing deep
and subsoiling; sowed one bushel Of
white Boughton wheat per acre. The
result was an average of thirty and one
half bushels of choice wheat per acre
Thus, you will see that the only manure
used to improve the land and get thirty
and one-half bushels of wheat where he
could only raise ten was to pillow under
deep a good crop of clover and subsoil.

A census of Warsaw, Indiana, has just been taken, its object being to obtain a city charter. It results in showing a population of little over twenty-five hundred, just enough to obtain it. An election has been called to decide the question, and will be held on the 18th. A large meeting was held in the Court house last night of those favorable to it. The citizens are about evenly divided on the matter.

Thursday morning, as Michael Harpster was going through the woods of Cyrus Beard, Plain township, Wayne, had in his possession a mare, which he offered for sale at various prices—so low that it aroused suspicion. Mr. Harpster left the woods and returned, bringing with him five other men. When they got to where the mare was, the man was not to be found, and is still at large. The mare is large dark bay, five or six years old, white feet behind, white front foot, small star in forehead, nice mane, with thin tail. Two blankets and a saddle were with the mare.

Particulars are received at Shanghai of fight in Formosa between savages and Chinese troops. Two Chinese officers ventured in January last to enter the region of the Botan aborigines, and were immediately killed. February 18th a body of 200 troops went from Hong Kong on the West Coast to retaliate. They burned one village and put the inhabitants to death, including old men, women and children. On their return they were surrounded and routed with a loss of 81 killed, among whom was the Chinese leader. The loss of the savages is estimated at 30. There is much excitement in China, and rumors of large forces to be dispatched to the scene.

Many a hardship and badge of con-
tempt has been changed to an honor by
using it discreetly and wesring il nobly.
The place of lady hostess at the head
of the table is said to have been first
assigned for reasons less creditable to
the men than we had supposed.


In Queen Elizabeth's time the fashion
came into vogue of placing the princi-
pal joints and pieces of meats at the
head of the table, above the salt, in
order that the chief guests might re-
gale their eyes with the promise OF
good cheer before them, and also be
conveniently served to the choicest cuts.
This custom involved the necessity of
carving the meats after they had reached
the table; therefore the ladies were
invited to sit at the head of the board,
that they might perform the service
which had before been delegated to the
professional carver.


1t was thus from no desire to compli-
ment the fair sex that woman was, in
the beginning, promoted to the most
honorable place at the table. It was
for the selfish convenience of her lord,
and not for her own dignity, that the
position was accorded to her and as,
in medieval society, she ministered to
her guests by preparing dishes for their
enjoyment, often bearing them to the
table herself, so she now, in the capac-
ity of carver, continued in the rank of
a servitor.


But, with the tact which is her dis
tinguishing characteristic, she has grad
ually converted the carver's stool into a
throne of state, and assumed the right
to preside over the company through
an Office which originally authorized
her only to help them with food.

Party in Detroit.


Shortly before II o'clock last night a
terrible tragedy was enacted OF the resi-
dence of Mr.. Nelson s. Whipple, No.
367 Lafayette street. A select party had
been given in honor of his daughters
birthday, and all the rooms of his hand
some residence had been thrown open
to receive the young lads and misses
who came as invited guests. The festiv-
tiles OF the evening were at their height.
The young people were engaged in vari-
GUS pastimes, some playing on the piano,
while merry dancers beat the time upon
the floor, others chatting gayly in groups,
running up and down the stairs, Or
strolling about ON the walk in front of
the house. Suddenly the loud report of
a gun and piercing shrieks were heard
to proceed from the bedroom at the
head of the stairs, which had been thrown
open as cloak-room, and cloud of
blue smoke hoated through the hall.
The startled and Mortified guests rushed
to. the stairway led by Mr.. Whipple,
who reached the landing on the second
floor just in time to receive the body of
Miss Frances Amsden, lovely and esti-
mable young girl, seventeen years of age,
who was sinking to the floor in dying
condition, her ife-blood pouring from
a ghastly wound In the head. In a very
few seconds after the report of the
gun she breathed her last. It appears
that while the others of the party were
amusing themselves below, Miss Amsden,
together with several other young ladies,
had entered the cloak-room at the head
of the stairs. A few minutes afterward
blanchard Whipple, young lad about
fifteen years old, came up for pillow to
be used in we'll known children's game,
and playfully commanded the girls to
run down stairs and play "pillow." !"
Miss Amsden In asportive mood snatched
the pillow from his hands and refused to
give it back. Young Blanchard then
brought out q double-barrelled shotgun
from a clothes press, and, pointing it at
her In mock tragic manner, repeated
his demand that she should give up the
pillow, at the same time attempting to
snatch it from her. The other girls were
frightened at this and ran out of the
room, which they had scarcely quilted
before the weapon was in some manner
discharged. The spectacle was terrible
one, and in the brilhantly-ighted house,
crowded with the young girls in their
white dresses, who had the moment be-
fore been SO mirthful and joyous, the
presence of death in such form seemed
doubly solemn. The body was taken
home. Her distracted parents were
there waiting to receive it, and their cries
of anguish were most heart-rending.
Thus ended social party which will re-
main an epoch in the lives of all who at
tended it.=Detr0it Tribune.

to proceed from the bedroom at the
head of the stairs, which had been thrown
open as cloak-room, and a cloud of
blue smoke floated through the hall.
The startled and mortified guests rushed
to the stairway led by Mr. Whipple,
who reached the landing on the second
floor just in time to receive the body of
Miss Frances Amsden, lovely and esti-
mable young girl, seventeen years of age,
who was sinking to the floor in dying
condition, her life-blood pouring from
a ghastly wound in the head. In a very
few seconds after the report of the
gun she breathed her last. It appears
that while the others of the party were
amusing themselves below, Miss Amsden,
together with several other young ladies,
had entered the cloak-room at the head
of the stairs. A few minutes afterward
Blanchard Whipple, young lad about
fifteen years old, came up for a pillow to
be used in a well-known children's game,
and playfully commanded the girls to
run down stairs and play "pillow."
Miss Amsden in a sportive mood snatched
the pillow from his hands and refused to
give it back. Young Blanchard then
brought out a double-barrelled shotgun
from a clothes press, and, pointing it at
her in mock tragic manner, repeated
his demand that she should give up the
pillow, at the same time attempting to
snatch it from her. The other girls were
frightened at this and ran out of the
room, which they had scarcely quitted
before the weapon was in some manner
discharged. The spectacle was a terrible
one, and in the brilliantly-lighted house,
crowded with the young girls in their
white dresses, who had the moment be-
fore been so mirthful and joyous, the
presence of death in such form seemed
doubly solemn. The body was taken
home. Her distracted parents were
there waiting to receive it, and their cries
of anguish were most heart-rending.
Thus ended a social party which will re-
main an epoch in the lives of all who at-
tended it.—Detroit Tribune.

The announcement of the withdrawal of several lines of steamers plying between this port and New York, particularly when viewed in connection with the stoppage of more than half the steamships running between the United States and Europe, suggests many conclusions which Northern businessmen should carefully read, ponder and inwardly digest.

In our opinion, the friends of De-
mocracy and representative govern
ment need waste bat little anxiety on

tive platforms Of Ohio and New York.

a secondary issue only, in so far as our
present depressed condition is cogent
argument with the people at large

be the case. Further discussion, fur
Their comparison of views, Will tend to
secure a better readjustment Of our
finances on a permanent basis, and the
Democracy will never be content with
any other.


The supreme issue with our Northern
brethren is to root out the corruption.
lists who have turned the temple of lib
erty into a den Of thieves. This was

the revolution of last fall This alone

| Carolina and Massachusetts,. This is
the one issue affecting all places and
classes alike, being national in its aim,
and palpable to Observation-Disclosures.
1t is a matter that touches every mans
pocket, and at the same time eyokes
every spark of honesty and virtue in
the land. As Wendell Phillips re-
marks, whole nation can attend to
but one matter at time, and the one
thing uppermost in the popular mind
is 20 scourge out the thieves that have
infested our high places with brazen
effrontery for years.


Among the hosts Of honest Repub-
licans who have no share in the spoils
of Office, there are thousands who will
refrain from voting or even support the
Democratic ticket, under an honest
conviction that their own party merits
rebuke and can be purified only by
displacement from power. They may
have little faith in Democratic princi.
pies or promises, yet they argue that
the latter will be on its good behavior
for a time, after which they hope for g
restoration of their own party, purified


by defeat. So strong is this feeling
against Credit Mobilierism and Whisky


Rings and Indian Rings and Navy

people believed the Democrats would


do no better, they would nevertheless
vote the Republicans out of power on
the principle Of rotation IN Office. II

they would insist on rotation in rascal.
ity even.


No cloudy divergences of financial
views will suffice to turn the people

sword-fish is heartily enjoyed, but in the
patronage.


In former times the Creoles and Indi-
ans of South America looked with horror
upon turtle, and yet in the United
States none but the rich enjoy the fare.


But, when we come to consider the IN-
sect races, we find that they furnish
more food delicacies than is generally
supposed. The grub of the palm weevil
is considered as something delicious. In
the West Indies, in Surinam, and the
Island of Mauritius the larvae of the
cocoanut beetles are enjoyed by the
inhabitants of British Guiana, and in
South America and Western Africa certain
mammoth beetles are eagerly de-
!
former years, have been sold for
English cabinets at the rate of ESQ; in
Australia, many worms, bred in decayed
wood, are collected for human food. Va-
rious members of the locust family are
now, and have been from time immeno-
rial, employed as food in various parts of
the world, and, as they live on vegetable
food, it is difficult to understand why a
mess of grasshoppers may not be as pala-
table as a dish of shrimps; curry of ants'
eggs is deemed luxury in Siam; various
kinds of water-bugs are eaten in Mexico;
butterflies in Australia are more highly
esteemed for their flavor than their
beauty; spiders form an article in the
list of Bushmen's dainties in South At-
rica, and roasted spiders are spoken of
as enjoyed by the people of New Cal-
e-donia; Lalande, the French astronomer,
having been fond of them—and Hum-
boldt tells us he has seen the centipede
eagerly devoured by the children in
South America.


In Italy cockchafers are candied and
served up with other confectionery, and
in Austria large wood ants are served up
and eaten alive.


The diversity of tastes prevailing in
different parts of the world in regard to
food would seem to confirm the proverb
that "one man's meat is another man's
poison." In very many instances, what
is highly esteemed in one country is al-
horred in another.


Milk as an article of food (except for
sucking babies) is loathed by the South
Sea Islanders. Goats have been intro-
duced into several of the islands, but the
people deride the settlers for using the
milk, and ask them why they do not
milk their sows. On the other hand,
dogs and rats are favorite articles of
food with them. As for pork, it is on
religious grounds that the Jews and Mo-
hammedans abstain from it, as the Hin-
dus of the East seem to have nearly an equa-
l aversion to it and the like prevailed
until lately in Scotland.


Maize or Indian corn has been intro-
duced into New Zealand by the mission-
aries, and the people cultivate and highly
esteem it. But their mode of preparing
it for food is, to civilized people, most
disgusting. They steep it in water until
it is putrid, and then make it into a kind
of porridge which emits an intolerable
stench.


Human flesh has been and still is eaten
in many parts of the world, and that by
the people considerably above the low
rank of Savages, such as those in the
Batta, who are said to have a writer's
language. And even in cannibalism
there are great diversities; some
eat their enemies and some their friends.


Herodotus relates that Persian King,
asked the Indian soldiers that were in
his service what reward would induce
them to burn the dead bodies of their
friends instead of eating them. They
replied by entreating him not to mention
anything so shocking.


On the other hand, the New Zealand-
ers—before their conversion, who seem
to have considered that the proper diet
of mankind is man—were once in the
habit of eating only their enemies.
Among the Australian savages it
is said that if a mother finds a young baby
troublesome to carry about, she will eat
it (although she will not allow any one
else to do so), under the full persuasion
that she merely deferred its birth, and
that the next child she bears will be
the
reappearance of the eaten one. When
demonstrated with, she will reply: "Oh
massa, he plenty come again!"


By some Arctic travellers it has been
asserted that the Esquimaux have been
known to eat their sledges when pressed
with hunger; but when we remember
that these sledges are made of froze-
n salmon, with skins sewed over them,
our wonder is modified; and, in an ex-
tremity, a piece of one sledge, washed
down with whale oil, might not be such a
dreadful tit-bit.

LOVERS OF MUSIC.
To the Editor:

Lovers of music in our city, enjoyed a rich treat last Thursday night, by the united talent of the Gallipolis Naomi and our own "Cornstalk." The air was melodious with their sweet and enlivening strains; the night, too, was most propitious for this union of music; the moon enhancing the charm by its witching light. We could but think how in spring all this to many of the interested promenaders, and that sweeter strains, it may be, were whispered to many ears and hearts as the music "floated on." And now a word specially for our own Band, as we are proud to call its members showing by their gentlemanly and temperate habits, and conduct, what a band may be in a community, and indeed, wherever represented, honoring themselves, and thus elevating the art. We think we are according only merited praise, when we call ours a "model Band." In connection with this, Mr. Editor, we would express our enjoyment and appreciation, and we know we are not alone in this, of the very appropriate and becoming manner, in which they recognized and honored the Anniversary of our National Independence, by their sacred and patriotic music. As "Old Hundred" pealed forth, we thought, yes, how fitting this, upon this sacred day, for the anniversary that has brought so many blessings to us as a people. And then how softened and subdued the strains, as "Hail Columnia" and other joyous airs, came wafted to us from the breezy hillside, convincing the respect and reverence of the performers for the Sabbath, that nothing loud or gay should mingle in the music-tones, whereby they would honor The Glorious Fourth, without the Sabbath stiffness, or disturb the most pious heart. It is an honor to the Cornstalk Concert Band.

A CITIZEN.

Leede fell and died almost instantly. German immediately left, but was stopped by Capt. Lem not far from the corner, and turned over to Officer Henkle.


THE INQUEST.


Early yesterday morning Dr. J. F. Hartigan made post mortem on the body at the central guardhouse, when he found that the ball had entered the upper portion of the right ventricle of the heart, following through and entering the margin of the left lung, and entered the right lung and lodged between the sixth and seventh ribs in the muscular tissue, about the same distance from the middle line of the body as at the point of entrance.


The coroner, Dr. Patterson, held the inquest at the guardhouse, at 10 o'clock.


Will A. Short testified that as he was coming out of the St. George dining saloon on 9th street, near F, he heard the report of a pistol; looked across the street and saw considerable commotion; crossed over in that direction and saw the prisoner, German, going down 9th street, swinging a pistol in his right hand in careless manner; saw the arrest by Capt. Lem, who took the pistol from him. The officer took the prisoner back into the saloon, where the proprietor identified him. Witness asked the proprietor what the trouble was, and he said that the men had got into some argument. The proprietor was at that time very much excited.


Mr. F. P. Lens testimony corroborated Mr. Short's.


THE PRISONER SORRY.


Officer Henkle testified to the facts of the case as above stated, and said the prisoner told witness that he was sorry; he did not influence of liquor; locked him up and went back; Leede was dead; identified the pistol; only one barrel empty.


Regey Major testified that he was putting in new gas fittings in the restaurant. The man who was shot, the prisoner, and two others took a drink—three beers and a whisky; the prisoner told him he was a liar; with that they clinched. Charley, the proprietor, then came in and grabbed prisoner by the collar and told him he wanted him to go out; with that they struggled to the kitchen, when they were parted by some men who came through the dining room. German came out, walked to the window where the other three were, and opened his coat and said "I am not hurt any, can lick a dozen such Dutchmen as them; damn it, look here" at the same time drawing pistol from his pocket. The pistol exploded and the shot took effect in one of his friends. The prisoner was facing the deceased when he drew the pistol and placed it over the left hand and raised the hammer, when it exploded. The prisoner left at once and the crowd came around.


Chas. T. Windholtz testified that about five o'clock he was busy in back room, came out to the bar and saw whole party there; told the barkeeper not to give the man German anything more to drink; he would not sell him anything at any time; then went back; heard the barkeeper speaking loud and calling for him (witness;) went there and they were scuffling; he separated them and told German to go out of the back way; two or three interfered and said let him alone and not make any fuss, and he let him go and sent the colored boy after the police; then went back into the ale vault, and while there heard the report of the pistol; ran in and saw German standing, and Leede sitting in the chair; German started out and witness followed and pointed him out to Capt. Lem, who captured him.


Louis T. Schenck, the barkeeper, detailed the particulars of the row, and said he heard the report of the pistol and saw Leede fall. Leede had been in the saloon about two hours; had smoked several cigars; thinks Leede drank with German.


J. W. Brown testified that he saw German standing in front of Mr. Leede, who was sitting in one corner of the room; heard a remark about pistol, and naturally turned his head and saw German standing with the pistol in his right hand with his arm extended; saw the flash and saw Leede fall; witness described the positions of the several parties; witness was about twenty feet away; did not hear the conversation; there were seven or eight persons in the barroom at the time.


Lillie Duvall testified that she saw the pistol in man's hand; did not identify the prisoner.


THE VERDICT.


Dr. Hartigan testified as to the result of the autopsy.


The jury returned verdict that deceased came to his death from wound of the heart, inflicted with pistol fired by the hand of Dennis German.


THE VICTIM, LEEDE,


was young man only 25 years of age, a native of Walten field, Hanover, where his parents still reside, and had been in this country several years. His general appearance was that of a well-to-do gentleman. He was a jeweler by occupation, and at the time of his death in the employ of Mr. John Y. Beiger, No. 902 street. Among those who knew him he bore an excellent character. He has a brother living in Chicago, who has been telegraphed for. He was a Royal Arch Mason, and held membership in Mount Vernon chapter, No. 3, and Lafayette Lodge, No. 2.


THE PRISONER, DENNIS GERMAN,


is a man about 30 years of age, five feet seven inches in height, dark complexion, black hair and eyes. He is a carpenter by trade, but did not work at his business. His reputation is bad. During the inquest yesterday he appeared to be completely broken down, and his appearance clearly indicated that he appreciated his situation.


A PARTNERSHIP SUIT.—On Saturday, Messrs. Shellabarger and Wilson filed bill in equity for Jonathan Taylor against J. S. Filbert, for an account. The bill states that the parties entered into a partnership in November, 1871, under the name of Taylor and Filbert for the execution of contracts in making and improving avenues, streets, &c, the profits and losses to be equally divided; plaintiff to be the financial manager for the procurement of money. The bill states that they obtained and executed a large number of contracts in this city and elsewhere nearly all being executed in the name of Filbert with complainant as surety.


The complainant states that there never has been any formal dissolution of the co-partnership, although Filbert, he is informed, on the 9th of March, 1874, published a notice to that effect; that the work done in Washington amounted to about $160,000 and for the purpose of prosecuting the work he negotiated loans to the amount of about $50,000, which was checked out by Filbert, who had the books. He charges that Filbert contributed no means or capital, but withdrew from the bank large amount of the money beside the assets, which he misapplied, about $35,000. He swears that on just settlement, excluding contracts in the name of Nandenburg, there will be due him $50,000; he swears that Filbert has paid out for purposes not in any manner connected with the business.

The Secretary of the Interior, the Commissioner of Indian Affairs, and their confederacies of the Indian Ring, appear to have taken alarm at the recent exposures, and are now striving to arrest further investigation by temporary expedient.
The Indian Commissioners whom Delano selected after the old board resigned in a body on account of the monstrous frauds which he protected, have asked the War Department to detail officers to inspect the supplies for certain tribes at Kansas City, Cheyenne, and Sioux City. But this does not meet the exigency at all. Nothing short of an examination of the supplies when delivered to the Indians and inspection of the cattle which they actually receive, will satisfy the public. The tricks and knavery of agents, contractors, and officials, all acting together in collusion, have become well understood.

A large portion of the plunder from this source is obtained by the substitution of inferior and short supplies for those which have passed inspection, between the points of final shipment and the delivery to the Indians. Sometimes the substitution takes place at the very agency where the goods are gathered for the tribe, so as to divert suspicion and thwart inquiry.

All confidence in an honest administration of Indian affairs has been withdrawn from the Interior Department. About three millions per year are estimated to have been stolen and squandered since Delano and his associates have run the concern. In five years they have drawn from the Treasury thirty-two millions for service which, for the same length of time under Lincoln, cost only sixteen millions, with one-fourth more Indians to feed than now exist in the United States.

This thieving system is made more insidious, because it has been carried on under the hypocritical pretence of protecting the Indians, and in the abused name of a peace policy. The practical effect of this scandalous treatment has been to confirm the red men in distrust of the white, to make him look with disfavor upon professions of religion, and instead of making him friend, to provoke his bitter enmity.

An amendment to the Indian Appropriation bill, requiring all sums voted for supplies to be expended by officers of the regular army, and contracts to be made as they are for the troops, will not only stop these disgraceful abuses, but break up the Indian Ring.

Other reforms can only come with a change of Administration in 1877, but this one may be achieved next winter in spite of the power represented in Congress by these plunderers. The Senate will of course resist any change like that suggested. But if the House will insist upon upright dealing with the Indians, public opinion will soon set the matter right and make the Senate recede from false position.

"I can get fifty women to Larry me,
within fifty miles of this village," said
man to me the other day, "but can't find
a woman anywhere who will come and help
my wife, and she is breaking down every
day." Yes, breaking down. Can anyone

season and out of season? She has four lit-
tle girls, the eldest six years and the
youngest six months. Her husband keeps
six cows and cultivates a farm of one hun-
dred acres, employing two hired men to aid
him. Three meals must be cooked daily
for a family of seven, not counting the
baby; four children washed and cared for,
the milk of six cows collected and butter
made, while the weekly washing and
ironing must be accomplished in some way
from four o'clock in the morning, until ten
and sometimes eleven o'clock at night, on
one pair of feet and one pair of hands perform
this labor, and now the tired body rebels,
and says: "This cannot be endured." A
coarse extra aid is not to be easily obtained
in midsummer, but it might have been pro-
cured early in the spring; it doubtless
would have been found had it been needed
to assist in the man's work.


Let me tell of another case: This
farmer and his wife have three children, all
under eight years. He employs two hired
men, boarding them, and he keeps eleven
cows. A woman comes to do the washing
and ironing, but that is all the assistance
the wife receives, excepting the few steps
her children save her. She must rise at
four in the morning and prepare breakfast
so that her husband and the hired men can
be in the field at five. Every other day,
however, one of the hired men remains to
do the churning for her, but this favor was
not allowed her until she threatened to call
in the doctor, to declare to her husband her
inability to do such hard work. Then it
was reluctantly conceded, although two
forty-pound firkins of butter were packed
each week; for our farmer prides himself
upon his herd of cows—pure blood Alder-
neys—and sells his butter at the highest
rates, carefully depositing the proceeds in
the bank, and rarely giving his wife so
much as a five-dollar bill of it. His last in-
junction to the husband as he departs to the
field: "John, come just as quick as you
can. Do not let Mrs. J. keep you for any-
thing else. Hay can't wait for women's
work." There are dishes to wash, milk to
skim, pans to scald, beds to make, children
to dress, baby to nurse, rooms to sweep,
and dinner to cook over the boiling hot
stove—and one woman to do it all.

It was like a blast of lightning, and sent in a long, reverberating peal of laughter. After that, I could not help contrasting the way in which the average landsman would give an order, with the mate's way of doing it. If the landsman should wish the gang-plank moved foot farther forward, he would probably say, "William, one of you push that plank forward, please," but pat the mate in his place, and he would roar out: "Here, now start that gang-plank for a lively now! What are you about, snatch it, snatch it! Where are you at again, again? Don't you hear me? Dash it, dash it! Are you going a-sheep over it, now? Heaving, vast heaving, I tell you! Heave it, heave it, clear a-stern! Where are you going with that tarrell toward it, for! Make you swallow it, you lazy dash-dash-dashed split between tired mud turtle and crippled heave-horse!"

I wished I could talk like that.

When the soreness of my adventure with the mate had worn off somewhat, I began timidly to make up to the humblest official connected with the boat—the Waterman. He made no advances at first, but I ventured to offer him a chalk pipe, and that softened him. He allowed me to sit with him by the bow bell on the hurricane deck, and in time he melted into converse with me. He could not well have helped it. I hung on his words and spoke so plainly that I felt honored by his trust. He told me names of his kin, and shared only landsman secrets with me. We drifted by in the solemnity of the night, under the twinkling stars, and in and by got on talking about him. He seemed over-sentimental for a man whose salary was six dollars a week, or rather he might have seemed so for an older man than I. But he drank in his words hungrily, and with faith that might have moved mountains if it had been applied judiciously.

What was it to me that he was soiled and seedy and fragrant with gin? What was it to me that his grammar was bad, his construction worse, and his diction so void of art that it was almost like a man strength in his conversation? He was a wronged man, a man who had seen trouble, and that was enough for me. As he mellowed into his plaintive story his tears dripped upon the linen in his lap, and I cried, too, from sympathy. He said he was the son of an English nobleman, either an earl or an alderman; he could not remember which, but believed he was born; his father, the nobleman, loved him, but his mother hated him from the cradle; and so while he was still a little boy he was sent to one of them old ancient colleges—he couldn't remember which—and by and by his father died and his mother seized the property and shook him, as he phrased it. After his mother shook him, members of the nobility with whom he was acquainted used their influence to get him the position of loblolly boy in ship; and from that point my Waterman threw off all tremnels of date and locality and branched out into a narrative that bristled all along with incredible adventures, a narrative that was so reeking with bloodshed and so crammed with hairbreadth escapes and the most engaging and unconscious personal vignettes, that I sat speechless, enjoying, relishing, wondering, worshipping.

It was a sore blight to find out afterward, that he was low, vulgar, ignorant, deceitful, half-witted humbug, an unvarnished native of the wilds of Illinois, who had absorbed wildcat literature and appropriated its manner, too. In no time he had wove a odds and ends of the mess into this yarn, and then gone on telling it as legends like me, until he had come to believing it himself.

MARK TWAIN.

darling's name-had been in poor health

grieved sadly over the loss of our only
child, year before, by scarlet fever, and |

case-startling, indeed, to the love with
which l cherished the bereaved and sor-
rowing mother. l had accordingly pre-

Summer there, wait for my Autumn trip

my business tour accompanied by my wife.

country travel, country fare and accommo-

ton of hearing Lucy murmuring her pray
ers, dear girl, but 1 am sure that before

busy at their spring work.


THERE will be communion services at
the Belmont street Presbyterian Church
tomorrow.


The voice of the organ grinder is
again heard in the land.


The entertainment given at School
Hall last night is spoken of in the high
est terms, and we regret very much that
our engagements were such as to prevent
us from attending it.


QUITE large number of our citizens
are at St Clairsville attending the trial
of the ownership of the public square.
The health of our city is good at pre-
sent.


SOME of the farmers in the vicinity of
Bellaire have commenced to plow.
EGGS are quite plenty in this market
at present, and yet they are selling at
twenty cents dozen. Butter is quite
scarce.


ANY one who has any settlements to
make with the Old Town Council, had
better do it tonight, or it will be forever
too late, as this will be their last night
for the transaction of business.
WE have no police items to report, as
not a single arrest was made yesterday.


THE mud on our streets has about
dried up.


The arguments in the case now before
the District Court at St. Clairsville, con-
cerning the Public Square of this city,
will most likely be concluded to-day.


Mr. V. T. MORGAN was some better
yesterday.


MR. JOHN CREE and wife, formerly a
resident of this county, but now of
Georgetown, Colorado are visiting
friends in this city. Mr. Cree
moved from Captina, in this
county, to Iowa in 1850 and re-
sided there ten years; he then removed
to Georgetown in 1860 and has lived
there ever since. Mr. Cree is a very in-
telligent and genial gentleman and
speaks in the most glowing terms of
Colorado and of Denver City as being
the Mecca of the nation. We wish Mr.
Cree and his good lady a pleasant visit,
and a safe return to their far off home.


MARTINS FERRY.


FRIDAY, April 9th, 1875, has been
marked in Martins Ferry's calendar as
one of the dullest days for local news she
has ever experienced.


WORK was commenced yesterday in
hauling away the gravel bank where the
new bank building is to be located.


A MEETING of the stockholders of the
new National Bank, is called for to-day,
at which time seventy per cent of the
stock subscribed will be paid in. The
bank will commence operations in a
very short time.


MESSRS. SPENCE, BAGGS & Co., will
make a very large shipment of stoves on
the Hudson to-day.


Dusty? We should say so. You know
Martins Ferry has a good deal of sand
in its clay, and it don't take long to
raise dust.


The efforts to build a suitable Town
Hall have not been abated yet; a
meeting of the stockholders of the Union
Hall Association will be held to-day
to decide upon location.


A PROMINENT lawyer of the village
was arrested yesterday afternoon for
using profane and abusive language on
account of the absence of witnesses;
Mayor Dean had not heard the case
when the reporter left.


BRIDGEPORT.


A YOUNG man named WM. Bed, came
near being seriously injured while at
work in Ferguson & Meads planing
mill yesterday. He was engaged in
trimming plank with circular saw,
when through some inadvertence, the
board was caught by the saw and thrown
with great force against the pit of his
stomach. It made him extremely sick
and caused him to quit work, but it did
no other damage.


The young man who was injured in
Z. J. Bags & Co.'s mill, on Thursday,
was somewhat better yesterday, although
he can by no means be said to be out of
danger.


THE soda fountains commenced siz-
zing yesterday. Fountain No. 1 has
been established in the store next to
McGill & Junkins.


BRIDGEPORT proper is not quite so
dusty as Martins Ferry; the soil is not
so sandy. For all of which Bridgeport
may feel thankful.


The whistle of the engines on the new
roads is expected to be heard before the
coming of hoar frosts.


THAT portion of Bridgeport commonly
called Etnaville refuses longer to furnish
sensations.
